The central idea

## A progression toward greater choice and direction in daily support

The surviving evidence does not show that one project formally became the next. It does show a progression of ideas toward greater choice and direction in how daily support could be organized.
:::

::: {.story-arc}
::: {.story-step}
::: {.story-step-no aria-hidden="true"}
01
:::

::: {.story-step-era}
Before the 1980s
:::

### Institution

For many people with very high physical support needs, institutional care shaped where and how daily life happened.
:::

::: {.story-arrow aria-hidden="true"}
→
:::

::: {.story-step}
::: {.story-step-no aria-hidden="true"}
02
:::

::: {.story-step-era}
Mid-1980s
:::

### Community

Creekview helped demonstrate that people requiring extensive assistance could live outside hospital.
:::

::: {.story-arrow aria-hidden="true"}
→
:::

::: {.story-step}
::: {.story-step-no aria-hidden="true"}
03
:::

::: {.story-step-era}
Around 1990
:::

### Self-direction

The documentary trail begins to show an explicit focus on people receiving home support acting as employers.
:::

::: {.story-arrow aria-hidden="true"}
→
:::

::: {.story-step .story-step-final}
::: {.story-step-no aria-hidden="true"}
04
:::

::: {.story-step-era}
1994–95 onward
:::

### CSIL

Public funding supports home care, while greater day-to-day choice sits with the person or their support structure within program rules and accountability requirements.
:::
:::

::: {.story-caution}
**Important:** this is a progression of ideas, not a claim that Creekview formally became ECPM or that ECPM formally became CSIL.
:::

:::
:::

::: {.story-shift}
::: {.story-section-inner}

::: {.section-intro}
::: {.eyebrow .eyebrow-light}
What actually changed?
:::

## Public responsibility remained. Day-to-day choice moved closer to the person.
:::

::: {.story-models}
::: {.story-model}
::: {.story-model-label}
Conventional delivery
:::

::: {.story-flow}
1. Public funding
2. Health authority or agency
3. Workers scheduled and managed
4. Person receives support
:::
:::

::: {.story-model .story-model-highlight}
::: {.story-model-label}
CSIL
:::

::: {.story-flow}
1. Public funding
2. Person, representative, or client support group
3. Workers scheduled and managed
4. Support organized around the person
:::
:::
:::

::: {.story-shift-note}
Current rules name three employer forms: the person, a CSIL representative, or a client support group. Those forms are documented in [Later evolution](history/evolution.qmd).
:::

:::
:::

### Leaving the institution

#### Creekview

Six men with high-level quadriplegia, most dependent on ventilators, moved from hospital into a community residence near False Creek.

[Explore the Creekview evidence →](history/creekview.qmd){.chapter-link}
:::

::: {.chapter-card}
::: {.chapter-card-head}
::: {.chapter-no aria-hidden="true"}
02
:::

::: {.chapter-era}
c\. 1990
:::
:::

### Becoming the employer

#### Enhanced Consumer Participation Model

A surviving bibliography records a training manual intended to help consumers of home-support services act as employers.

[Explore the ECPM evidence →](history/ecpm.qmd){.chapter-link}
:::

::: {.chapter-card}
::: {.chapter-card-head}
::: {.chapter-no aria-hidden="true"}

:::

### Direct funding becomes public policy

#### CSIL design and pilot

Later official records describe a 1994 pilot and province-wide availability in 1995, while the archive preserves disagreement about the exact founding chronology.

[Explore the CSIL pilot evidence →](history/csil-pilot.qmd){.chapter-link}
:::

::: {.chapter-card}
::: {.chapter-card-head}
::: {.chapter-no aria-hidden="true"}
04
:::

::: {.chapter-era}
2008 → today
:::
:::

### An established BC program

#### Later evolution

CSIL develops into an established mechanism for eligible people to receive public funding and direct their own home support. Later records also document client support groups and CSIL representatives.

[Explore later evolution →](history/evolution.qmd){.chapter-link}
:::

::: {.eyebrow}
A model with continuing relevance
:::

## More than three decades of experience with person-directed, publicly funded care

CSIL demonstrates that publicly funded home support can be person-directed rather than provider-managed. The person — and, where necessary, a representative or client support group — can take a greater role in organizing support.

::: {.story-close}
That experience is worth understanding as British Columbia considers how more people can be supported safely at home.
:::
